clusters.name: product · content · company · diverse
sample: This feature activates on beginning-of-sequence tokens followed by generic, informational opening phrases typical of web content—headlines, dates, company descriptions, product reviews, and promotional material that establish factual or commercial context.

This feature activates on beginning-of-sequence tokens that introduce generic, factual, or commercial text—such as product descriptions, news headlines, company information, and dated content—representing the start of diverse informational or promotional passages.

This feature activates on beginning-of-sequence tokens followed by text opening patterns typical of web articles, product descriptions, news snippets, or promotional content—essentially generic introductory material from diverse online sources.

This feature activates on the beginning-of-sequence token immediately followed by diverse, generic opening text—news articles, product descriptions, company blurbs, event listings, and promotional content—representing the start of standalone informational or commercial documents.

This feature detects the beginning of diverse web-sourced text documents, particularly the opening lines of articles, product descriptions, event postings, and promotional content that typically appear in indexed web pages or scraped content collections.

clusters.name: product · news · company · content
sample: This feature detects the beginning-of-sequence token (<bos>) immediately followed by diverse, encyclopedic or factual opening content (product descriptions, news headlines, company information, dates, ratings), characteristic of web-scraped or reference material corpus text.

This feature activates at the beginning of text sequences (immediately after <bos>) that introduce factual, informational, or promotional content such as product descriptions, news snippets, company information, or event announcements.

This feature activates on the beginning-of-sequence token (<bos>) immediately followed by diverse, everyday informational text fragments—product descriptions, news headlines, dates, company information, and promotional content—suggesting it detects the onset of generic web-scraped or encyclopedic prose.

This feature activates on the beginning-of-sequence token (<bos>) immediately followed by diverse, factual opening text across multiple domains (product descriptions, news leads, dates, company information, ratings), suggesting it tracks the onset of generic informational or commercial content.

This feature activates on the beginning-of-sequence token (<bos>) followed by diverse introductory content types, detecting the onset of new document or text passages across various domains (product descriptions, news, dates, promotional content, reviews).

clusters.name: greetings · informal · particularly · hello
sample: This feature activates on casual opening greetings and salutations at the beginning of text, particularly "Hello," "Hey," "Hi," and similar informal address tokens that initiate conversational or personal communication.

This feature detects opening salutations and introductory phrases that begin documents or webpages, particularly greetings like "Welcome," "Hello," "Published," and "By" that signal the start of a new communicative context or piece of content.

This feature activates on opening framing devices at the beginning of text, particularly "Welcome" greetings and structural markers like brackets or metadata tags that introduce or frame content (reviews, patches, links, updates, multilingual text).
This feature detects the formulaic opening phrase "Welcome to" that introduces websites, services, or communities, typically appearing at the start of landing pages or welcome messages.

This feature tracks expressions of gratitude and thanks, particularly when they appear at the beginning of sentences or messages in formal/semi-formal contexts like customer service responses, acknowledgments, and appreciation statements.

clusters.name: person · possessive · activates · first
sample: This feature activates on the first-person singular pronoun "I" appearing at the beginning of a text passage (after the start-of-sequence token), particularly when initiating personal narratives, anecdotes, or subjective claims.
This feature fires on first-person narrative or memoir-style writing that begins with "I" statements expressing personal experiences, observations, or accomplishments.

This feature activates on first-person singular pronouns and contractions ("I", "I'm", "I've", "I was") that initiate personal narrative statements or subjective claims, particularly when the speaker is sharing experiences, opinions, or accomplishments.
This feature activates on first-person narrative voice, specifically the pattern of "I" at the beginning of sentences or clauses that introduce personal experiences, observations, or statements.

This feature activates on possessive constructions and institutional/organizational entity markers, where a proper noun or entity name is followed by possessive indicators (apostrophe-s, "'s") or appears in a role-defining context before a description of what that entity manages, operates, or is responsible for.

clusters.name: activates · particularly · names · nouns
sample: This feature detects the beginning of proper nouns and branded names (Chain, Galvan, Silvio, Citgo, Vodafone, Balotelli, Naucalpan, Poly, Pub, Law, Motion) where capitalized words are split mid-token or appear at text boundaries, tracking how the model processes named entity recognition and capitalization patterns.

This feature activates on capitalized words or proper nouns that appear at the start of text following the beginning-of-sequence token, often marking titles, names, or product identifiers that introduce content categories.
This feature fires on capitalized words or word fragments that appear at the start of text segments, particularly nouns used as headers, titles, or category labels in lists and product descriptions.

This feature activates on product/service category descriptors and noun phrases that specify what type of item or offering is being presented (e.g., "Haul," "Kit," "Inventory," "Tour," "Apartment," "Review"). These words function as classifying labels that immediately follow the main subject noun or brand name in commercial, product, or travel listing contexts.

This feature detects capitalized topic headers or section titles that introduce business/organizational categories, services, or subject domains (recruitment, configuration, fitness, upgrades, consulting, advertising, etc.).

clusters.name: prepositions · temporal · spatial · activates
sample: This feature activates on the word "when" used as a conjunction or temporal marker introducing a conditional, circumstantial, or explanatory clause that provides context or reasoning for a preceding statement.

This feature activates on the phrase "In the/a/an" at the beginning of sentences, particularly tracking the common prepositional opening pattern that introduces temporal, locational, or contextual frames.

This feature activates on spatial proximity descriptors and distance/location prepositions that indicate how close something is to a nearby landmark or destination (e.g., "from," "to," "walk," "minutes," "miles," "located").

This feature activates on the preposition "in" or "In" appearing at the beginning of clauses or sentences, often after punctuation or at sentence starts, functioning as a locative or temporal connector.

This feature tracks the preposition "in" when used to specify geographic location or jurisdiction—particularly in contexts establishing where institutions, businesses, or events are situated within a specific place (city, region, country).
